seedance25.summary: Browse copy-ready Seedance 2.5 video prompts with writing tips, featured examples and the full prompt text — native audio, 30-second multi-shot scenes.
overview: Seedance 2.5 is ByteDance Seed team's flagship video model, released on July 31, 2026. Where earlier clip generators produced a few seconds of silent footage, Seedance 2.5 generates up to 30 seconds of video with synchronized sound and multiple connected shots in a single pass — closer to a scene generator than a clip generator. It is the model most of our recent cinematic, action and lifestyle entries were made with.

The release centers on control: it accepts dozens of multimodal reference assets (images, video and audio), keeps characters and locations consistent across shots, and can edit a specific time range of an existing clip — changing a character, an action or a line of dialogue while leaving the rest untouched. A faster, cheaper Seedance 2.5 Flash variant followed on November 12, 2026. In our library the model leans heavily toward cinematic and realistic looks, with action, portrait and vlog-style prompts close behind.

tips.title: Write numbered scenes with time ranges
tips.body: The strongest 2.5 prompts in our library read like a shot list: "Scene 1 (0–5 seconds)… Scene 2 (5–12 seconds)…". The model plans camera and narrative across the full 30 seconds, so giving each beat its own time window keeps the story on schedule instead of letting one shot eat the whole clip.

tips.title: Declare the film look up front
tips.body: Open with format and grade — aspect ratio, frame rate, "photorealistic, shot like a high-budget film", then the color treatment (for example cold teal-blue shadows against warm shop-light highlights) and film grain. Prompts that set this grammar first hold a consistent look across every later shot.

tips.title: Give each reference asset one job
tips.body: 2.5 accepts many references at once. The cleanest prompts assign each asset a single role — face, outfit, location or motion — and say what it should NOT inherit from the image. That prevents the model from blending a wardrobe reference's background into your scene.

tips.title: Draft cheap, finish high
tips.body: Since September 2026 a Draft mode generates a 480p preview first and only renders the 1080p final once you are happy. Iterate on structure and timing at draft quality, then commit — the same workflow the Flash variant is built for.

examples.title: Three Friends By A Pool At Night
examples.comment: A quiet, almost wordless drama told across a dressing room and a teal-lit pool. Notice how each scene gets a time window and a lighting motif — warm vanity bulbs against cold pool light — and the emotion is carried by blocking rather than dialogue.

examples.title: Four Thugs Surround A Girl In Tokyo
examples.comment: A 30-second street-action short written like a real production brief: 24fps, 16:9, a cold-teal/warm-yellow grade, visible breath in winter air. The environment details — vending machines, glowing signage, a parked white car — are what make the backstreet feel filmed rather than rendered.

examples.title: A Baby Dragon Wears A Woolly Hat
examples.comment: A family-friendly fantasy built from numbered scenes: shearing a sheep, then knitting its wool into a giant hat for a baby dragon. A good template for storytelling prompts where each scene must hand a prop or a character to the next.

faq.question: What is Seedance 2.5?
faq.answer: Seedance 2.5 is ByteDance's multimodal video generation model, released July 31, 2026. It generates up to 30 seconds of video with native synchronized audio and multiple connected shots in one pass, accepts up to 50 multimodal reference assets, and supports timestamp-level editing of existing clips.

faq.question: How is Seedance 2.5 different from Seedance 2.0?
faq.answer: Seedance 2.0 (February 2026) introduced unified audio-video generation with clips up to 15 seconds. Seedance 2.5 doubles the single-pass length to 30 seconds, greatly expands reference handling, and adds region-level editing controlled by timestamps, plus native support for more than 10 prompting languages.

faq.question: What is Seedance 2.5 Flash?
faq.answer: Flash is the accelerated, lower-cost variant of Seedance 2.5, released November 12, 2026. It generates 4–30 second clips roughly twice as fast at a lower price, aimed at high-frequency iteration and draft workflows.

faq.question: Where can I use Seedance 2.5?
faq.answer: It runs inside ByteDance's consumer products — Jimeng (Dreamina) and Doubao — and is available to developers through the Volcano Engine API (BytePlus internationally). Prompts in our library link back to the source post so you can see which surface each clip was made on.

seedance2.summary: Browse copy-ready Seedance 2.0 video prompts — timestamped beats, handheld realism and multi-shot action, with the full prompt text and source clips.
overview: Seedance 2.0, released February 12, 2026, was the model that moved AI video from silent clips to unified audio-video generation: one model takes text, image, audio and video as input and produces multi-shot clips up to 15 seconds with sound generated together with the picture. It remains the largest single collection in our library, and the range is wide — cinematic action, fantasy battles, handheld vlog realism and tightly timed comedy beats.

Because it understands references across modalities, the community built a distinct prompting dialect around it: asset handles like @image1 lock a character's face or a specific outfit, beat sheets with timestamps (0:01, 0:03, 0:08…) choreograph the action, and "shot on an iPhone" prefixes summon convincing handheld imperfections. Seedance 2.5 has since extended the same ideas to 30 seconds and timestamp-level editing, but 2.0's prompt patterns still transfer directly.

tips.title: Choreograph with a timestamped beat sheet
tips.body: Many of the best 2.0 prompts are written as a timeline: "0:01 — the captain lights up; 0:05 — the raft starts hissing; 0:08 — passengers slide into the water". Explicit beats give the model a pacing contract, which is why comedy and action entries use them so often.

tips.title: Ask for camera imperfections, not just realism
tips.body: The handheld-style prompts that read as real phone footage spell out the flaws: focus hunting between subject and background, a 0.2-second defocus when the body leans in, rolling shutter, compression noise, white-balance drift. "Ultra-realistic" alone rarely gets you there — naming the artifacts does.

tips.title: Separate identity references from wardrobe references
tips.body: Use one asset handle for the face and body, and separate handles for outfit, glasses or hairstyle, stating that each reference contributes only that attribute. This is the community's standard fix for identity drift when a character changes clothes mid-clip.

tips.title: Keep beat sheets inside the 15-second window
tips.body: 2.0 tops out at 15 seconds per generation. Write beats that fit, or plan two generations and cut them together — prompts that ask for 30 seconds of story in one 2.0 pass tend to rush the ending.

examples.title: Captain Lights Cigarette On Sinking Raft
examples.comment: A comedy short written as a captain's log with timestamped beats. The joke lands because the prompt schedules the escalation — calm cigarette, hissing raft, sliding passengers — second by second instead of describing a generic disaster.

examples.title: She Offers A Slice Of Strawberry Cake
examples.comment: A selfie-style food clip that reads as genuine front-camera footage: breathing sway, focus hunting between face and cream, warm indoor light against cold glass reflections. A masterclass in specifying imperfection rather than quality.

examples.title: Sorceress Battles Armored Giants In Desert
examples.comment: Straightforward epic fantasy: one hero, one army, one clear power effect (glowing red energy, fire waves, dust storms). Shows that a single strong visual premise, clearly staged, beats a crowded scene description.

faq.question: What is Seedance 2.0?
faq.answer: Seedance 2.0 is ByteDance's unified multimodal audio-video model, released February 12, 2026. It accepts text, image, audio and video inputs and generates multi-shot clips up to 15 seconds with native sound, at up to 4K output.

faq.question: Does Seedance 2.0 generate sound?
faq.answer: Yes. Audio is generated jointly with the picture — dialogue, effects and ambience stay synchronized with the action — rather than being added in a separate post-production step.

faq.question: Should I write prompts for Seedance 2.0 or 2.5?
faq.answer: The prompt dialect transfers: asset handles, beat sheets and look declarations work on both. Choose 2.5 when you need up to 30 seconds, heavier reference stacks or timestamp-level editing; 2.0 remains a solid choice for 15-second multi-shot clips and is where most of our library's examples were generated.

pixverse.summary: Browse copy-ready PixVerse V6 video prompts — image-to-video, dance and portrait clips with native audio, plus writing tips and full prompt text.
overview: PixVerse V6 is the current clip-generation model from PixVerse (AIShi Technology), released March 31, 2026. It generates 1–15 second videos up to 1080p with native audio — dialogue, effects and ambience produced together with the picture — and can switch between wide, medium and close-up shots inside a single generation. A higher-fidelity V6 Max variant joined the family in October 2026.

V6's sweet spot is publish-ready social content: image-to-video portraits, dance clips synced to a beat, POV horror and product shots. The image-to-video and reference-to-video modes ranked second globally on Artificial Analysis's leaderboards at release, and the platform's free tier and low per-second pricing make it a common first stop for creators testing a prompt before rendering it on a pricier model. In our library, cinematic, action, fashion and dance prompts dominate the PixVerse collection.

tips.title: Let the reference image carry the look
tips.body: In image-to-video mode, don't re-describe the person's appearance — the reference already fixes it. Spend the prompt on motion and expression: a head tilt, a glance back to the camera, hair moving naturally. The portrait entries in our library follow exactly this split.

tips.title: Write audio cues into the prompt
tips.body: V6 generates sound with the picture, so describe what should be heard — dialogue lines, "SFX: rain, distant traffic", or the music a dance should follow. Beat-synced dance prompts work by stating that footwork, hips and gestures must lock to the track's rhythm.

tips.title: Choose the delivery aspect ratio before generating
tips.body: Set 16:9, 9:16 or another target ratio up front rather than cropping afterwards. V6 frames the subject for the chosen canvas, and a vertical composition planned from the start survives the feed better than a cropped wide shot.

tips.title: Draft at 360p/540p, deliver at 1080p
tips.body: Per-second pricing scales with resolution. The cheap tiers exist precisely for iteration: validate motion and timing at 360p or 540p, then re-render the keeper at 1080p. Review the audio take before publishing — native voice casting can still miss on multi-character scenes.

examples.title: Mirror Selfie In Wardrobe Mirror
examples.comment: A textbook image-to-video prompt: the reference photo fixes the person and the room, while the text directs only small, believable motions — a smile, a head tilt, adjusting hair — with explicit attention to natural hand and finger movement.

examples.title: Ten Second Dance Synced To Beat
examples.comment: Shows how to ask for music-synced motion: every body part — hands, hips, footwork — is told to synchronize with the background track, and the dress and hair are asked to move with each step. The physics details are what sell the dance.

examples.title: Ghost Woman Approaches Through Dark Hospital
examples.comment: First-person POV horror driven by camera behavior: a flashlight sweep down a deserted corridor, a figure appearing at distance, the camera turning to flee. The prompt directs the viewer's body, not just the scene — a pattern that works well for game-style clips.

faq.question: What is PixVerse V6?
faq.answer: PixVerse V6 is PixVerse's video generation model released March 31, 2026. It creates 1–15 second clips up to 1080p with native audio and multi-shot continuity, from text, a starting image, first/last frames, or 2–7 reference subject images.

faq.question: What is the difference between V6 and V6 Max?
faq.answer: V6 Max, released October 2026, renders the same 1–15 second, 360p–1080p format at higher fidelity and drops V6's style presets. Choose V6 for fast iteration and preset-driven looks, V6 Max when the clip is the final cut.

faq.question: Does PixVerse V6 generate audio?
faq.answer: Yes — dialogue, sound effects and ambience are generated natively with the video. Describe the sounds you want inside the prompt; and review the result, because voice casting on multi-character scenes can still be inconsistent.

faq.question: Is PixVerse free to use?
faq.answer: The PixVerse app offers a free credit tier, and API pricing is per generated second with cheaper 360p/540p drafts. That combination is why many creators prototype a prompt on PixVerse before rendering the final version elsewhere.

minimaxh3.summary: Browse copy-ready MiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3) video prompts — omni-modal references, native stereo audio and 2K output, with tips and full prompt text.
overview: MiniMax H3 — also known as Hailuo 3 — is MiniMax's omni-modal video model, launched July 31, 2026, with the 33B-parameter H3-Base weights published under a community license on August 3, 2026. It reads text, images, video and audio as one context and generates video with native stereo sound, up to 2K resolution and 15 seconds per clip, making it the strongest open-weight video model released to date.

What distinguishes H3 in practice is reference understanding: you can hand it up to 9 images, 3 video clips and 3 audio clips and describe how they relate — this face, that motion, this voice — instead of splitting the job across separate tools. Reviewers consistently highlight its motion-graphics discipline (stable on-screen text, restrained effects), which is why our H3 collection leans toward cinematic commercials, product shots, title reveals and stylized anime montages.

tips.title: Describe how references relate, not just what they are
tips.body: H3's omni-modal context is its superpower. Instead of listing assets, write the relationships: "Picture 1 fixes the character's face; the reference video supplies the camera move; the audio clip is the voice she speaks with." The timestamped reference prompts in our library show this pattern at full strength.

tips.title: Structure commercial prompts as fields
tips.body: Many H3 prompts are written as JSON-like blocks — duration, aspect_ratio, style, then the scene description. For product ads and title sequences this keeps the deliverable's constraints separate from the creative description, and makes the prompt easy to reuse across products.

tips.title: Use it where text and motion must stay clean
tips.body: H3 earns its reputation on motion graphics: kinetic titles, logo stings, UI-style animation. Ask for restrained, physically grounded motion and specify the exact on-screen text; reviewers find it notably more stable here than most video models.

tips.title: Budget for the audio take
tips.body: Sound is generated in the same pass as the picture — specify dialogue, ambience and music explicitly, then listen before publishing. Voice casting and lip-sync are good but not infallible, especially with several speakers in one scene.

examples.title: A Giant Shadow Passes Over The City
examples.comment: A structured prompt (duration, aspect ratio, style fields) that stages an ordinary overcast city before an enormous shadow crosses it. The documentary-style restraint — natural grey daylight, authentic traffic — is what makes the impossible event feel witnessed.

examples.title: Ultra Realistic Hazelnut Spread Commercial
examples.comment: A premium food-commercial prompt: extreme close-up, slow-motion spread, glossy swirls with visible hazelnut pieces. Exactly the product-shot territory where H3's texture rendering and controlled motion pay off.

examples.title: Anime Opening With Pixel Art Effects
examples.comment: A music-video montage written as 30 numbered poses with hard cuts, demanding the same identity, outfit and location throughout. A strong example of using explicit shot-by-shot structure to keep a stylized sequence consistent.

faq.question: What is MiniMax H3?
faq.answer: MiniMax H3 (also called Hailuo 3) is MiniMax's omni-modal video model, launched July 31, 2026. It understands text, image, video and audio references in one context and generates up to 15-second clips at up to 2K with native stereo audio.

faq.question: Is MiniMax H3 open source?
faq.answer: The 33B-parameter H3-Base weights were published on August 3, 2026 under the MiniMax H3 Community License, with task checkpoints for frame-conditioned and reference-driven workflows. It is open-weight rather than fully open-source, and the hosted API offers options the base weights do not.

faq.question: What is the difference between H3 and H3 Max?
faq.answer: H3 Max is the faster variant released August 30, 2026, aimed at speed-sensitive workflows (it also added a 480p tier on fal.ai). The standard H3 targets maximum quality with 768p and 2K output.

faq.question: How long can a MiniMax H3 video be?
faq.answer: A single generation runs up to 15 seconds; the Extend tool can continue a clip to roughly 30 seconds. Aspect ratios span 21:9 to 9:16 at 24fps, with 32kHz stereo sound generated in the same pass.

kling4flash.summary: Browse copy-ready Kling 4.0 Flash video prompts — reference-locked characters, continuous-take action and native audio, with tips and full prompt text.
overview: Kling 4.0 Flash is the fast tier of Kling 4.0, Kuaishou's fourth-generation video model family. Flash opened to early users on September 28, 2026, and the full Kling 4.0 launched on October 15, 2026 — the release that doubled single-pass length to 30 seconds, added 4K HDR output, dual-channel stereo audio with lip-sync in more than 10 languages, and up to 10 keyframes plus an omni-reference stack of images, videos and subjects.

Flash trades resolution for speed: 3–20 second clips at 720p, with the same reference-control DNA as the full model. That makes it the iteration workhorse of the Kling family — and our early Kling 4.0 entries show exactly what the family is being used for: reference-locked character action, comedy sketches with precise timing, and found-footage creature shots. Prompts written for Flash carry straight over to full Kling 4.0 when you need the 4K finish.

tips.title: Lock identity and props to numbered references
tips.body: Kling 4.0's omni-reference accepts several assets at once. The pattern that works in our library: "Use @image1 as the character's exact identity, face and hairstyle; use @image2 as her exact sword. Maintain perfect consistency throughout." One asset, one job, stated as a hard lock.

tips.title: Declare the continuous take explicitly
tips.body: For chase and action pieces, spell out "one unbroken continuous shot, zero cuts, zero hidden edits, zero transitions" and keep the action relentless across the full duration. Without that contract the model may insert cuts that break the illusion of a single take.

tips.title: Ground fantasy in a real camera
tips.body: The kaiju and creature prompts that convince are written as amateur camcorder footage: preserve the reference street's landmarks, match the creature's scale against buildings, and let the camera behave like a panicked operator. The format is the special effect.

tips.title: Iterate on Flash, finish on 4.0
tips.body: Flash renders 720p faster and cheaper; the full model adds 4K HDR, stereo audio and the 30-second ceiling. Validate blocking and timing on Flash, then re-run the winning prompt on Kling 4.0 for delivery.

examples.title: Rica Battles Gods And Monster Army
examples.comment: Opens with a character-and-weapon lock: one reference for Rica's exact identity, another for her sword, with consistency demanded throughout. The battle is then staged against a defined environment — grassland, hills, a towering deity — so scale stays readable.

examples.title: Kaiju Rampage Shot As Amateur Camcorder Footage
examples.comment: A 30-second creature rampage written as found footage: preserve the supplied street's brick storefronts and water tower, match the monster exactly, keep its scale immense relative to buildings. The camcorder framing is what makes it terrifying rather than cartoonish.

examples.title: Camera Chases Bicycle Through Rain
examples.comment: A rainstorm courier chase that demands one absolutely unbroken shot — zero cuts, zero hidden edits, zero teleportation — across the full 15 seconds. The clearest example in our library of the continuous-take contract.

faq.question: What is Kling 4.0 Flash?
faq.answer: Flash is the fast variant of Kuaishou's Kling 4.0 family, in early access from September 28, 2026. It generates 3–20 second clips at 720p with text, image and omni-reference inputs, trading resolution for speed and lower cost.

faq.question: How is Kling 4.0 different from Kling 3.0?
faq.answer: Kling 4.0 (released October 15, 2026) doubles single-pass length from 15 to 30 seconds, adds up to 10 keyframes, an omni-reference stack of up to 15 assets, 8,000-token prompts, 4K HDR output and stereo audio with lip-sync in more than 10 languages.

faq.question: Does Kling 4.0 generate audio?
faq.answer: Yes. The full model produces dual-channel stereo audio with multilingual lip-sync, so dialogue and sound are part of the generation rather than a post step. Flash clips are typically iterated silently and finished on the full model.

faq.question: Where can I use Kling 4.0?
faq.answer: Through Kling AI's own site (klingai.com), with API access rolling out after launch. Our Kling 4.0 Flash entries link to their source posts so you can see the exact workflow and settings each creator used.
